draft.title: Social and moral reform
card: Augustus believed Rome's upper classes had grown selfish and were having too few children. In 18 BC and again in 9 AD, laws were passed to change how they lived.

The laws pushed upper-class men and women to marry and have children. Those who stayed unmarried or childless could lose some rights to receive inheritances, while those with children gained advantages in a public career.
Adultery became a crime to be tried in a public court, not just a family matter. Punishments included exile and the loss of part of a person's property.
The aim was to rebuild the old values and the strength of the elite families, which supplied Rome's senators and officers. Many Romans disliked the laws, and they were hard to enforce.
draft.remember: Augustus used law to push the elite towards marriage, children and fidelity, as a way to restore traditional Roman values.

a.q: Which of these was a main aim of Augustus's marriage laws?
opts: To increase the number of children born to the upper classes
To stop slaves from being freed by their owners
To reduce the number of men serving in the army
To raise taxes from citizens living in the provinces
a.why: The laws targeted the upper classes, who Augustus thought were having too few children. Freeing slaves, army numbers and provincial taxes were not the aim of these laws.
a.clue: Think about who the laws were aimed at and what Augustus thought was wrong with them.

b.q: Livia's friend Marcus, a senator, is married but has been unfaithful. How would the Augustan laws have treated his conduct?
opts: As a public crime, with punishments such as exile
As a private family matter, left to the household
As a minor offence, punished with a small fine only
As a religious duty, to be handled by the priests
b.why: Augustus made adultery a crime tried in a public court, with penalties such as exile and loss of property. Before this it had mostly been dealt with inside the family, which is why the tempting second option is wrong.
b.clue: What changed about who dealt with adultery?

a.best: To increase the number of children born to the upper classes

b.best: As a public crime, with punishments such as exile

problems.detail: Under the lex Julia de adulteriis, a married man's infidelity was a crime only if his partner was another man's wife or a respectable unmarried woman. Sex with a slave or a prostitute was not punished. The question says only that Marcus 'has been unfaithful', so the answer could be wrong. It hides the law's double standard between husbands and wives.

The card treats adultery as one simple crime for anyone. It does not say that the law defined adultery around the married woman, so wives and husbands were not treated the same. This leads students into the flawed premise in question b.
